Pairwise-comparison leaderboards (Chatbot Arena, MT-Bench, sports ratings) are Bradley–Terry fits whose published uncertainty is a bootstrap CI. A CI answers "would another sample of the same process reorder the models?". Results for C1–C6 on the 91 data sets (Arena-55k and Arena single-turn; MT-Bench human; MT-Bench GPT-4 judge; 17 Arena-prompt LLM judges; 69 NBA seasons 1947–2015). All numbers are in `results/*.csv` of paper-repo `dev` (synced d202c30); scripts in `code/`. Pairs are model pairs; k* is a verified upper bound on the minimum number of alterations (an exact refit reverses the pair), found by search; the paper may not call it "the minimum".

**C1 (common scale / Q ≈ null).** Q = k*·g_max/gap is about 1.1 (median over pairs, 0.78–1.2 for delete; 1.1–1.3 crowd/LLM flip) and does not move with z for crowd/LLM; NBA flip Q rises with z (1.6 → 2.1 for z 1–8) but so does the same-graph null. Real-minus-null Δ(log Q, z∈[1,8]) lies inside the ±0.15 equivalence margin in **every** data set and both families (design means: delete −0.02…0.00, flip −0.01…+0.04; `real_minus_null.csv`). Largest: Arena-55k flip +0.056 [0.013, 0.099] — "within the margin, not exactly on it". So the finding is "F/z collapses because it is close to a first-order identity"; the null (k_null_pred) reproduces k* at the median to within ~2–6 % in the stratified table (`k_ratio_med`, 0.98–1.06). The lead (counts + null + prediction) stands; F is a gauge.
Equal-N scaling (10 units, 4 designs, `fragility_vs_N.csv`): k*/N falls with N with log–log slope −0.33…−0.51 (so k* ∝ N^0.5–0.7), F/z stays ≈ 0.9–1.1. Three units (MT-Bench GPT-4, NBA 1990/2015) have too few z∈[1,8] pairs at the largest and smallest sizes: NaN there, not zero.

**C2 (adversarial vs random).** Random deletion/flip essentially never reverses a pair at the adversarial budget: at k* the mean reversal probability is ~0.1 % (Arena-55k delete; `search_quality.csv` random row), and in the survival table random curves stay at ≈1.0 over the whole budget grid (up to 30 % of N), for every design. Adversarial survival of CI-separated pairs (published CIs) for median data set, delete: crowd 0.64 at 0.25 % of N, 0.04 at 1.2 %; LLM-judge 0.69 / 0.05; expert (MT-Bench human, N=3355) 1.00 until 2.7 % then 0.36 at 13 %; sports 1.00 until 1.2 %, 0.81 at 2.7 %, 0.01 at 6 %. So in absolute counts crowd/LLM data are far more fragile than sports/expert only per unit of N; in SE units they are alike (see C1/C4). Caveat: the Wilson intervals treat pairs as independent.

**C3 (CI-separated survive).** CI separation does not protect against a targeted adversary at small fractions of N in the large crowd and LLM sets (above), but separated pairs survive every random budget. Top-1 vs top-2 (`top1_conclusions.csv`): median k* to lose the top place — crowd 5.5 (Arena-55k: 2 deletions, z = 0.07), LLM judges 16 (z 2.2), MT-Bench human 91 (z 2.9), NBA 4 (z 0.6). The Arena top-1/top-2 pair is not CI-separated at all.

"Design" is confounded with data set (one expert set, two crowd sets), so claims about expert/crowd as designs rest on one and two data sets, respectively; write that.

shown.message:
All the result tables are now final and synced to paper-repo `dev` (d76146b). I closed figtab-repo's request #2 a little early, before a push failure forced me to shrink one file; the details are below.

- **Survival curves:** `survival_curves.csv` had been missing every LLM judge and every NBA season. The builder looked up files by names like `judge:X`, but the files are named `judge_X`. It now covers all 91 data sets.
- **File size:** the corrected file was 27 MiB, over the repo's 20 MiB limit, so the push was rejected. The repo copy now keeps only what the figures draw (published separation, the separated subset, the `frac` and `se` axes, about 3 MB). The full grid is written to `$BT_RESULTS/tables_full`.
- **For figtab-repo:** I closed #2 with a comment saying the file was final, before the push was rejected. I didn't post a correction. The reduced file still holds everything Fig. 3 draws.
- **Results for story-repo:** the C1–C6 interpretation is in story-repo#7. I corrected one number in it: random deletion at k\* flips a pair about 0.04% of the time, not 0.1%.
- **`REPRODUCE.md`:** it now discloses four things: k\* is a verified upper bound, the LP candidate is not certified, which analyses were not run, and designs are confounded with data sets.
- **Commitment:** I added a status note to #3.

The analyses I did not run are the insertion family, Arena-140k and slices, WebDev Arena, Rao–Kupper/Davidson, and NBA home advantage. The equal-N scaling covers 10 of the 91 data sets, not all of them.
